0.title: Mission Control
0.learn: Cyber Law deals with rights, responsibilities and legal consequences in the digital world. Technology gives us possibilities; Cyber Law asks when those possibilities are permitted, responsible and supported by evidence.
0.why: This lab begins with the principle CAN ≠ MAY. You will learn through simulated incidents, not by memorizing sections first.
0.remember: Technology tells us what is possible. Cyber Law asks what is permissible—and who is responsible.
0.author: Dr. Mohammad Amir Khusru Akhtar, Faculty of Computing & Information Technology, Usha Martin University
questions: Rights, responsibilities and legal consequences in digital activity
Technical capability does not automatically equal permission

1.title: Browser Revealed
1.learn: Browsers expose some environment information to web pages and place sensitive capabilities such as precise location behind permissions. A permission decision is only one part of the privacy question.
1.why: After access is granted, questions remain: why is data collected, how is it used, how long is it kept, and who receives it?
1.remember: CAN access → MAY access → HOW may it be used?
questions: Any future use is automatically acceptable
The browser may remember the permission, but purpose and responsible use still matter
Capability, permission and later use are different questions
Screen size is private banking data

2.title: Permission ≠ Capability
2.learn: An app may be technically capable of requesting many device permissions. Good decisions ask whether each permission is actually needed for the stated function.
2.why: Consent is meaningful when the request is understandable and proportionate to the purpose.
2.remember: Do not grant five permissions for a one-permission job.

3.title: The Unlocked Phone
3.learn: A device being unlocked makes access technically possible. It does not automatically mean the owner has permitted you to read private messages or use the account.
3.why: Cyber Law often turns on authorization, purpose, conduct and context—not merely whether a system was technically accessible.
3.remember: An open door is not an invitation.
questions: Only that access may be technically possible
Reading private messages without permission raises:
No concern if nothing is deleted
Leave it and seek permission if needed

4.title: Password ≠ Permission
4.learn: Authentication asks whether credentials are valid. Authorization asks whether the person using them is permitted to perform the action.
4.why: A working password proves that the credential works; it does not prove that you are entitled to use the account.
4.remember: Having the key does not mean you have permission to enter.
questions: Before using another person's account, verify:

5.title: OTP: One Number, One Decision
5.learn_title: An OTP is an authorization secret
5.learn: One-time passwords are often used to approve logins or transactions. An unsolicited caller asking for an OTP is a strong warning sign.
5.why: Attackers often exploit urgency and trust rather than technical weaknesses.
5.remember: No genuine urgency should make you surrender an authentication secret.
questions: A caller asks for your OTP to 'cancel fraud'. Best response:
End call and verify using official bank channel
Urgency in a message should make you:

6.title: Phishing Detective
6.learn: Phishing messages imitate trusted organizations and create urgency to make you click, disclose credentials or authorize payment.
6.why: The strongest defense is often a pause: inspect sender, domain, context and the requested action.

7.title: URL X-Ray
7.learn_title: Read the domain from right to left
7.learn: Attackers can place trusted-looking words inside subdomains or paths. You must identify the actual registrable domain instead of reading only the first familiar name.
7.why: A deceptive URL can look convincing while still pointing to a completely different organization.
7.remember: A trusted word inside a URL does not make the domain trustworthy.
questions: In google.com.example.com, the training lesson is that the controlling base domain is closest to:

8.title: HTTPS ≠ Genuine
8.learn: HTTPS helps protect the connection between your browser and the domain shown. It does not prove that the operator, offer or purpose is honest.
8.why: A fraudulent website can also use HTTPS.
questions: A phishing site can use HTTPS:
Domain + independent legitimacy of the request

9.title: Fake Login Laboratory
9.learn: A fake login page can visually copy a real service. The critical checks are the actual domain, how you reached the page, and whether the request is expected.
9.why: Never test an unverified page with real credentials.
9.remember: Appearance is easy to copy. Identity must be verified.
questions: Close and open official bookmark/site independently

10.title: Social Engineering Room
10.learn_title: The target may be the human, not the machine
10.learn: Social engineering manipulates trust, authority, fear or urgency. Messages may pretend to be from a Dean, bank, friend, HR or support desk.
10.why: Independent verification through a trusted channel breaks the attacker's story.
10.remember: Verify identity outside the message that created the urgency.
questions: Share less than half the password

11.title: Deepfake Courtroom
11.learn: Synthetic media can be harmless, deceptive or harmful depending on consent, labeling, impersonation, context and likely harm.
11.why: A short scenario often does not justify an automatic criminal-law conclusion. Good cyber-law reasoning identifies the concerns and the missing facts.
11.remember: AI can create the content; humans remain responsible for how it is used.
questions: A clearly labeled consensual parody is generally:
A realistic fake used to request money raises:
Assess consent, context, harm and evidence

12.title: Fake Instagram
12.learn_title: Your identity can be copied without your account being hacked
12.learn: A fake account may reuse your name, photograph and social relationships to deceive others.
12.why: The first response should preserve evidence, contain harm, secure real accounts, warn contacts and report through appropriate channels.
12.remember: Preserve first. Protect next. Report appropriately.
questions: First priority after discovering a fake profile:
If money is lost, response should become:

13.title: Cyberbullying Scenario
13.learn_title: Digital harm can be repeated and amplified
13.learn: Online harassment can spread quickly, persist through copies and affect real people. Responsible response includes support, evidence preservation and appropriate reporting.
13.why: Retaliation may escalate the situation and destroy useful context.
13.remember: Do not become part of the harm while trying to stop it.
questions: Best response to repeated abusive group messages:

14.title: Public ≠ Free
14.learn_title: Visible online does not mean ownerless
14.learn: Publicly accessible images, code and text can still be protected by copyright or subject to license conditions.
14.why: Permission to view is different from permission to reuse, modify, redistribute or claim authorship.
questions: A public image with no license is:

15.title: Copy–Paste–Submit
15.learn_title: Open source is not 'claim as mine'
15.learn: A license may allow reuse under conditions, but academic integrity separately requires honest attribution and compliance with assignment rules.
15.why: Legal permission to reuse code does not automatically make it acceptable to submit as your original work.
15.remember: License answers reuse rights; integrity answers honest authorship.
questions: MIT-licensed code may be reusable under its terms, but can you submit it unchanged as your own original work?

16.title: Evidence Desk
16.learn_title: A screenshot is a clue, not the whole case
16.learn: Digital evidence should be interpreted in context: source, timestamp, surrounding messages, metadata, original file and chain of handling can matter.
16.why: One artifact can be genuine yet still misleading if cropped, incomplete or detached from context.
16.remember: Evidence answers questions only when you ask what it actually proves.
questions: A screenshot alone always proves identity:
Original file + time + source + surrounding messages
What does this prove and what does it not prove?

17.title: Metadata Detective
17.learn_title: Files carry context beyond visible content
17.learn: Metadata can contain timestamps, dimensions, device labels and other context. But metadata can be missing, stripped, generated or altered.
17.why: A difference between Created and Modified time does not automatically prove malicious tampering.
17.remember: Metadata is evidence, not automatic truth.
questions: Created and Modified times differ. Does that prove criminal tampering?
Best conclusion from one metadata field:

18.title: Hash Witness
18.learn: A cryptographic hash converts data into a fixed-length fingerprint. A tiny change in the input normally produces a very different hash.
18.why: Matching hashes can support integrity checks; a mismatch shows that the compared bytes differ, but not who changed them or why.
questions: If one character changes, SHA-256 will typically:

19.title: IP Address ≠ Person
19.learn_title: Network evidence is not automatic identity
19.learn: Multiple devices can share one public IP address through NAT. Attribution may require timestamps, device/session logs and other evidence.
19.why: Choosing a person from one IP address can create a serious attribution error.
19.remember: An IP address can be a clue. It is not a human fingerprint.
questions: Three devices behind NAT can share:

20.title: Delete Button Myth
20.learn_title: Deleting from one view is not erasing every copy
20.learn: A message may disappear from your inbox while copies, logs, backups, recipient devices or audit records remain elsewhere.
20.why: Deletion can also remove evidence you may later need.
questions: Deleting a message guarantees every copy is gone:

21.title: UPI Fraud Simulator
21.learn: Payment scams often pressure users to scan a QR, enter a UPI PIN, reveal an OTP or 'refund' money without independent verification.
21.why: Verify the transaction in your own trusted banking/UPI app and use official support channels.
21.remember: Do not authorize a payment to 'receive' money.
questions: Someone says 'scan QR and enter PIN to receive refund'. Best response:
Verify independently; do not authorize under pressure
UPI PIN should be entered when:
You knowingly authorize a transaction in your trusted app

22.title: ₹10,000 Beat the Clock
22.learn: After an unauthorized financial transaction, useful actions include preserving transaction details, securing affected accounts, contacting the bank/payment provider and using official cyber-financial-fraud reporting promptly.
22.why: Delay can reduce opportunities for containment or fund tracing.
questions: After unauthorized debit, useful first item to preserve:
Should you delete the fraud SMS first?

23.title: 1930 Reporting Drill
23.learn_title: A report is stronger when facts are organized
23.learn: For a simulated cyber financial fraud, prepare transaction amount, bank/payment service, transaction ID/UTR, date/time, suspect identifiers and relevant evidence.
23.why: Organized facts reduce confusion when time matters.
23.remember: Evidence prepared before the call saves time during the call.

24.title: Complaint Builder
24.learn_title: Good complaints separate what happened from what you think happened
24.learn: A factual statement, an observation, an inference and an allegation are not the same thing. Good incident reporting labels them clearly.
24.why: This prevents overclaiming and helps investigators understand what is directly supported by evidence.
24.remember: Facts first. Evidence second. Inference clearly labeled.
questions: '₹7,500 left my account at 23:41' is best treated as:
Chronological facts + evidence + clearly labeled inference

25.title: Incident Response Room
25.learn: Response often involves preserving evidence, containing the incident, changing compromised credentials through trusted channels and reporting appropriately.
25.why: Retaliation and unnecessary deletion can make the situation worse.

26.title: Cyber Law Courtroom
26.learn: Short digital scenarios are often incomplete. A careful decision distinguishes potentially unlawful conduct, lower-risk conduct and cases where there is not enough information.
26.why: Legal reasoning is strongest when it avoids automatic guilt and identifies missing facts.
26.remember: Not enough information can be the most accurate answer.
questions: When facts are incomplete, best option may be:

27.title: Red Team vs Law Team
27.learn: A technical weakness may be testable, but safe security testing requires explicit authorization, approved targets, scope, time window and data-handling rules.
27.why: Technical curiosity does not create legal authority.
questions: Production target outside scope should be:
Red Team vs Law Team teaches:

28.title: Screenshot ≠ Whole Truth
28.learn: A screenshot can be authentic yet incomplete. Full chat, timestamp, original file, metadata and source account may change what the screenshot appears to show.
28.why: Evidence quality depends on provenance, context and what is missing.
28.remember: Before judging the screenshot, inspect the case around it.

29.title: Who Did It?
29.learn_title: Reconstruct events before naming a person
29.learn: Login logs, session IDs, device events, messages and network records can be correlated to build a timeline. Correlation increases confidence but does not remove the need for careful inference.
29.why: A strong investigator separates evidence from identity claims.

30.title: Can Attack ≠ May Attack
30.learn: A student may discover a technical possibility such as an endpoint, parameter or response behavior. The next step is not exploitation—it is checking authorization and scope.
30.why: This is the central boundary between safe learning and unauthorized activity.
30.remember: The more capable you become, the more important authorization becomes.
questions: Discovering a possible weakness gives you permission to exploit it:
Am I authorized and within scope?
How far can I push it?

31.title: Final Cyber Mystery
31.learn: A scholarship phishing email leads to a look-alike login, account session change, fake social profile, AI voice message, a friend's payment, deleted messages and a shared campus IP.
31.why: You must reconstruct the timeline, distinguish proof from inference, preserve evidence, secure accounts and choose appropriate reporting actions.
31.remember: The final skill is not memorization—it is disciplined judgment.

32.learn: The final assessment checks whether you can apply the core CyberLex principles across privacy, authorization, phishing, evidence, AI, attribution and incident response.
32.why: Completion is based on demonstrated learning, not clicking through screens.
32.remember: You learned Cyber Law through hands-on investigation.
